story: In New Orleans, Dave Bartholomew and Professor Longhair brought Afro-Cuban instruments and the clave pattern into rhythm and blues. Longhair's way with rhythm became a basic template of funk. When Little Richard left secular music in 1957, some of his band joined James Brown and the Famous Flames. By the mid-1960s Brown put the weight on the first beat of every bar instead of the backbeat. The change began with "Out of Sight" in 1964 and "Papa's Got a Brand New Bag" in 1965. In 1990 Brown explained it: "I changed from the upbeat to the downbeat." His arranger Alfred "Pee Wee" Ellis credited drummer Clyde Stubblefield's New Orleans drumming as the basis of modern funk. With "Cold Sweat" (1967), "Mother Popcorn" (1969) and "Sex Machine" (1970), Brown dropped even the twelve-bar blues. In New Orleans the Meters had R&B hits with "Cissy Strut" in 1969. George Clinton's bands Parliament and Funkadelic mixed it with jazz and psychedelic rock. Many early disco songs and performers came straight from funk. From the late 1980s hip-hop artists sampled funk records, and James Brown is said to be hip-hop's most sampled artist.

disagreements: Origin: record says Augusta and Cincinnati; the Funk article names neither. It places the roots in New Orleans R&B ('Longhair's rhythmic approach became a basic template of funk') and says funk 'originated in [[African-American]] communities in the mid-1960s' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk?action=raw). Augusta/Cincinnati is not contradicted, but it is unsourced here.
Began: record says 1965; the article dates Brown's shift from his 1964 single 'Out of Sight' and his 1965 hits. Consistent within a year.

Ended: record says 1980; the article says 'The 1970s were the era of highest mainstream visibility for funk music' and that by 'the latter half of the 1980s, pure funk had lost its commercial impact' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk?action=raw). The source suggests a later fade than 1980.
notes: All sentences from the English Funk article. Sentence 4 credits the downbeat shift to Brown by the mid-1960s; the record's marker 'the one' is supported. The Little Richard sentence relies on the article's own wording that his band members joined Brown after his 1957 exit; the article attributes the 'first to put the funk into the rhythm' credit to Brown himself.
